paras: The lynching of Frank and John McDonald took place at Menominee, Michigan, on the night of September 27, 1881, when a mob broke into the county jail and killed the two men, who were held on a charge of stabbing two brothers named Kittson. A crowd that a Menominee dispatch put at over 500 people, "composed mostly of Frenchmen, Indians and half-breeds," dragged the prisoners through the street and hung their bodies from a tree beside the house where the quarrel had begun. Most papers carried only a brief wire item datelined Oconto, Wisconsin, which garbled the names and in some copies put the jail at Oconto.

According to a Menominee dispatch, the McDonalds were ex-convicts who had been out of the state prison for only two weeks. Two days before the dispatch was sent, at a "disreputable house" on the outskirts of the village, they got into a row with Willie Kittson, described as "a half-breed, about 23 years old." When Norman Kittson and Tommy Dunn led Willie away, the McDonalds attacked them in the street; Willie was stabbed to death, and Norman received knife wounds the dispatch expected to prove fatal. Sheriff Barclay jailed the two men and posted extra guards.

About 10 o'clock that night the mob overpowered the sheriff and his guard and broke open the jail door and cell with timbers, sledgehammers and axes. The prisoners were pulled out with long ropes around their necks and dragged about three-quarters of a mile to the house where the row had started. By the dispatch's account they were dead "long before" their bodies were suspended from a tree there, after which the house was set on fire and burned to the ground.
Citizens who answered the sheriff's call arrived too late to resist. The bodies hung from the tree until the next morning, when the authorities took them down.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecutions appears in the coverage. In mid-October the Manitowoc Pilot reported that the father of the "McDonald boys" had come to Menominee with a United States marshal, vowing to spend every cent of his $300,000 to punish those who lynched his sons.

Most papers learned of the lynching from a special to the Milwaukee Republican datelined Oconto, which ran on September 29 in the Chicago Daily Tribune under "Two Murderers Lynched" and in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer under "The McDonald's Lynched." The item called the men "two roughs" who had "brutally murdered two brothers" and said only that they had been taken from jail and lynched. Over the next ten days it was copied from Nevada and California to weeklies in Arkansas, Kansas, Tennessee and Louisiana.

In the copying, the brothers' surname appeared as "Kibbon," "Mitson," "Kilson," "Kitson" and "Ketson." Some versions turned "McDonald, cousins" into two men named "McDonald and Cousins," and the Eureka paper's copy said the men were taken "from the jail here," placing the lynching at Oconto.

The detailed account came from a Menominee dispatch of September 28, printed under the headline "Murder and Lynch Law" in the Crawford Avalanche of Grayling, Michigan, and the Kenosha Telegraph in Wisconsin. It stressed the McDonalds' prison records but said they were dragged "mercilessly." A Trenton, New Jersey, paper condensed it to the killing, by "a crowd of 500 men," of two cousins who had murdered "two half-breed Indians." The Eaton Democrat called the McDonalds "desperate characters," while an October 7 dispatch from their home city, printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune, said they "bore good characters" there.

The Eureka copy of the wire placed the lynching at Oconto, while the Menominee dispatch and later summaries placed it at Menominee. The Menominee account is the stronger evidence, sent from the scene and naming the sheriff, the victims and the mob's route. The Montana New North-west dated the lynching to the 28th rather than the 27th.

The wire said two brothers were murdered, while the Menominee dispatch reported one dead and one dying; only the Eaton Democrat said the men were "clubbed, shot and hanged." Most copies called the McDonalds cousins, but the Manitowoc Pilot described both as sons of the same father.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank and John McDonald
bases: A mob broke into the jail at Menominee, took out two prisoners held for a fatal stabbing and killed them, hanging the bodies from a tree (A17, A14, A13).

A mob of over 500 overpowered the sheriff, took Frank and John McDonald from jail and killed them in retaliation for the stabbing of the Kittson brothers (A17, A14); every report calls it a lynching (A1, A2, A19).

An Oconto-datelined wire special (A1, A2), a detailed Menominee dispatch (A17, A14), a hometown dispatch (A20) and a Manitowoc follow-up (A23) agree that the two McDonalds were taken from jail and lynched.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Two Murderers Lynched', 'Two Roughs Lynched'; the wire item called the men 'two roughs' who 'brutally murdered' two brothers and added no comment.
The Menominee account, 'Murder and Lynch Law', stressed the McDonalds' prison records but said they were dragged 'mercilessly' and that resistance was impossible.
The Eaton Democrat called the McDonalds 'desperate characters'; a hometown dispatch in the Chicago Tribune said they 'bore good characters'.
